content: Women living with asymptomatic or mild HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 1 or 2) can use the following hormonal contraceptive methods without any restrictions: combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs), combined injectable contraceptives (CICs), contraceptive patches and rings, progestogen-only pills (POPs), progestogen-only injectables (POIs) such as depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) and norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN), and implants containing levonorgestrel (LNG) or etonogestrel (ETG) (MEC Category 1). These women can also generally use the LNG-intrauterine device (LNG-IUD) (MEC Category 2). Women living with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) can also use the same hormonal contraceptive methods without restrictions, including COCs, CICs, contraceptive patches and rings, POPs, POIs (DMPA and NET-EN), and LNG and ETG implants (MEC Category 1). However, they should generally not initiate the use of the LNG-IUD (MEC Category 3 for initiation) until their condition improves to asymptomatic or mild HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 1 or 2). Women who already have an LNG-IUD inserted and later develop severe or advanced HIV clinical disease do not need to have the IUD removed (MEC Category 2 for continuation). These women should be closely monitored for pelvic infections. Women taking any nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) can use all hormonal contraceptive methods without restrictions, including COCs, contraceptive patches and rings, CICs, POPs, POIs (DMPA and NET-EN), and LNG and ETG implants (MEC Category 1). Women using antiretroviral therapy (ART) containing efavirenz or nevirapine can generally use COCs, patches, rings, CICs, POPs, NET-EN, and implants (MEC Category 2). Women using newer non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) such as etravirine and rilpivirine can use all hormonal contraceptive methods without restrictions (MEC Category 1). Women using ritonavir-boosted antiretrovirals (ARVs) can generally use COCs, contraceptive patches and rings, CICs, POPs, NET-EN, and LNG and ETG implants (MEC Category 2) and can use DMPA without restrictions (MEC Category 1). Women using ARV medications can generally use LNG-IUDs (MEC Category 2), provided their HIV clinical disease is asymptomatic or mild (WHO stage 1 or 2). Women with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) should generally not initiate the use of the LNG-IUD (MEC Category 3 for initiation) until their condition improves to asymptomatic or mild HIV clinical disease. However, women who already have an LNG-IUD inserted and later develop severe or advanced HIV clinical disease do not need to have the IUD removed (MEC Category 2 for continuation). Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated in all adolescents living with HIV, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. ART should also be initiated in all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count, and continued for life. Mothers living with HIV should breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue breastfeeding for up to 24 months or longer, similar to the general population, while being fully supported for ART adherence. Practicing mixed feeding is not a reason to stop breastfeeding in the presence of ARV drugs. The use of amniotomy alone for the prevention of labor delay is not recommended. WHO recommends that safe abortion services for women living with HIV who want a voluntary abortion should be the same as for all women. WHO also recommends the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine for girls aged 9–13 years. Girls receiving their first dose of the HPV vaccine before the age of 15 can use a two-dose schedule, with an interval of six months between doses. Immunocompromised individuals, including those living with HIV, and females aged 15 years and older should receive three doses (at 0, 1–2, and 6 months) to be fully protected. Mothers living with HIV and healthcare workers can be reassured that ART reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission in the context of mixed feeding. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended, but mixed feeding is not a reason to stop breastfeeding if ARV drugs are being used. In 2015, 18 million women aged 15 and older were living with HIV, constituting 51% of all adults living with HIV. Adolescent girls and young women are particularly affected, accounting for 60% of young people aged 15–24 living with HIV and 58% of newly acquired HIV infections among young persons in this age group. Women living with HIV often face inequitable access to quality health services and multiple forms of stigma and discrimination. They are also disproportionately vulnerable to violence, including violations of their sexual and reproductive rights. The right to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) is an integral part of the right to health. To ensure the SRH and rights (SRHR) of women and girls living with HIV, attention must be paid to critical dimensions such as human rights, gender equality, responsive health systems, empowerment, and engagement of women in policy development, and strengthened monitoring and accountability procedures. This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for the SRHR of women living with HIV, particularly in resource-limited settings, and good practice statements to increase access, uptake, and quality of SRH services, improve human rights, and promote gender equality. It consolidates new and existing recommendations and good practice statements related to the SRHR of women living with HIV into one document.
